Loving v. Virginia. In 1967, the Supreme Court struck down all remaining state laws criminalizing interracial marriage. The case began when Richard and Mildred Loving, a Black woman and white man, were prosecuted under Virginia's Racial Integrity Act for their marriage. They were convicted and exiled from the state for twenty-five years.

The Supreme Court voted unanimously to overturn their conviction. Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote that marriage is a fundamental liberty and that restricting it by race violates equal protection under the 14th Amendment. Sixteen states still had miscegenation laws on the books at the time. Warren's decision invalidated all of them at once.

The Lovings' case became a symbol of both personal freedom and the waning days of Jim Crow legal scaffolding. The decision was one of the broadest civil rights victories of the era, with no sustained dissent and little organized opposition. It established that the right to marry is a fundamental constitutional protection that cannot be abridged on racial grounds. Richard and Mildred Loving had lived in exile from their home state, unable even to visit as a married couple. The Supreme Court's decision finally allowed them to return to Virginia with dignity.
